analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and its companion 2010 health-and-education law entirely, with no replacement.
analysis.headline: All 52 Senate sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, including the Majority Leader, but the bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 in their entirety, effective 180 days after enactment, restoring the law as it stood before 2010. That would end the ACA's insurance subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and protections for people with preexisting conditions, while also erasing the taxes the ACA placed on high incomes and medical devices and restoring bank-issued federally guaranteed student loans. The bill contains no replacement coverage provisions of any kind.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners, who would stop paying the ACA's 3.8% tax on investment income and 0.9% Medicare payroll surtax on income above roughly $200,000–$250,000. Medical device makers, who would stop paying the 2.3% excise tax. Student loan companies and guaranty agencies, whose bank-issued guaranteed-loan business the 2010 reconciliation act ended. Insurers, freed from the ACA's coverage requirements, though they would also lose the mandate-driven customer base.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, device makers, loan middlemen

how_it_helps.text: Repealing the two acts erases the taxes they created to fund the ACA, including the 3.8% net investment income tax and the 0.9% Medicare payroll surtax on high incomes, cutting taxes concentrated on the wealthiest households.
The Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 imposed a 2.3% excise tax on medical devices; full repeal of that act removes the tax.

The same act ended the decades-old system of federally guaranteed student loans issued through private banks and moved lending to the Direct Loan program; repealing it restores the bank-middleman system.
Repeal restores the pre-2010 rules for individual insurance markets, eliminating the ACA's coverage mandates and insurance regulations on a 180-day timetable.

analysis.who_pays: People who would lose ACA coverage and protections on a 180-day timetable: households receiving premium subsidies, people covered by the Medicaid expansion, people with preexisting conditions who would again be denied or priced out of coverage, young adults on their parents' plans, and seniors whose Medicare drug benefits and preventive-care coverage under the ACA would lapse. None of the lost coverage is replaced anywhere in the bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: ACA beneficiaries and people with preexisting conditions

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the entire ACA with no replacement provisions, so insurance subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, preexisting-condition protections, dependent coverage to age 26, and Medicare improvements all lapse 180 days after enactment.

Repealing the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act also rolls back its non-health provisions, restoring a student loan system that routed federal lending through private banks at greater cost to taxpayers and borrowers.

Supporters framed full repeal as removing taxes and mandates, but the bill's own text sets a hard 180-day effective date and offers no transition, bridge coverage, or successor program for the millions covered under the ACA.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow mainly to a narrow set of taxpayers and industries — high earners paying the ACA's surtaxes, device makers, and student loan middlemen — while its costs fall on the tens of millions of people who got coverage or protections through the ACA. Because the bill includes no replacement for any of the coverage it repeals, the drawbacks clearly outweigh the benefits for ordinary households.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Ted Cruz introduced the bill with 51 Republican cosponsors, but the Senate Finance Committee never acted on it, and no vote ever came in either chamber before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 2, 2015, and read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.
Fifty-two senators — the sponsor and 51 cosponsors — all Republicans, signed onto the bill, including Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell.
The bill would have repealed the Affordable Care Act and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 in full, effective 180 days after enactment, restoring the prior law.
No further action was taken after the referral for the remainder of the 114th Congress; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people covered by the ACA — subsidy recipients, Medicaid expansion enrollees, and people with preexisting conditions — are no worse off, because the repeal never advanced and nothing changed for them.

for.name: Ted Cruz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the ObamaCare Repeal Act on February 2, 2015, a full repeal of the ACA and the 2010 reconciliation act effective 180 days after enactment.

for.name: 51 of 54 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making every Senate backer a Republican.

for.name: Mitch McConnell
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but never brought it to the Senate floor for a vote during the Congress.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 2, 2015 and took no further action — no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: His caucus's 46 seats were enough to sustain a filibuster, meaning any repeal could not reach the floor without Democratic support that no Democrat offered.

sides.party_line_note: All 52 Senate sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, including the Majority Leader; no Democrat supported the bill, and with 60 votes needed to end debate in the Senate, the 46-seat Democratic minority could have blocked any repeal vote.

industries.note: Repealing the ACA erases the 3.8% net investment income tax and the 0.9% Medicare payroll surtax on income above roughly $200,000–$250,000, the taxes that helped fund the ACA's coverage expansion. Their gain comes from removing funding for the coverage and protections the rest of the bill strips away.
The 2010 reconciliation act imposed a 2.3% excise tax on medical devices; repeal removes it. The tax helped fund expanded coverage that the same repeal eliminates.

Repeal frees insurers from the ACA's coverage requirements, community-rating rules, and spending floors, but it also removes the individual mandate that supplied them with millions of healthy, paying customers. They lose guaranteed enrollment and guaranteed rules at the same time.

industries.industry: Student loan companies and guaranty agencies
industries.note: The 2010 reconciliation act ended federally guaranteed lending through private banks and moved all student lending to the Direct Loan program; repeal restores the bank-middleman system, whose fees and subsidies came at taxpayer and borrower expense.

The ACA required manufacturers to discount brand-name drugs for seniors in the Medicare coverage gap and expanded the insured customer base; repeal removes the discount obligation but also the millions of newly insured customers. The two effects run in opposite directions.
